nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: One Massachusetts pharmacist is supervising one certified pharmacy technician and two pharmacy technicians. Another employee holds a current pharmacy technician license but is assigned only to the front register and initially performs no professional pharmacy support. During a rush, the manager directs that employee to enter prescription data. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: While the employee performs only cashier duties and no professional pharmacy support, the employee may be excluded from the support-personnel ratio.
Once the employee begins prescription data entry, the cashier label no longer keeps the employee outside the ratio.
The resulting four-person support team is permitted because every member holds a pharmacy personnel credential.
The employee remains excluded for the entire shift because the schedule lists the employee as a cashier.
The data-entry assignment must satisfy technician scope and supervision rules independently of the numerical ratio analysis.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: A community pharmacy receives an individually signed referral for a patient to enter a collaborative drug therapy management program. The document lists the patient's name and address, primary diagnosis, authorized comorbid diagnoses, and detailed treatment instructions. It does not state the patient's known allergies and contains no statement that the patient gave written informed consent. The pharmacist notes that the affiliated hospital often begins inpatient collaborative management through a consultation request that does not contain those two items. What is the best conclusion for the community-pharmacy referral?

choices.text: It is sufficient because a signed referral and specific treatment instructions replace the need for allergy and consent information.
It is sufficient if the hospital's consultation process would accept the same document.
It is incomplete because a community CDTM referral must include known allergies and a statement of written informed consent, in addition to the other required patient-specific information.
It is incomplete only if the patient has a known allergy that would change the treatment instructions.
It may be completed by treating the hospital's consultation request as an incorporated attachment, even though that request contains neither missing item.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: During prospective drug utilization review, the pharmacy system flags a clinically significant conflict. A certified pharmacy technician tells the pharmacist that the technician can clear the alert under the pharmacy's protocol and that documentation is needed only if the prescriber is called. Which statements correctly describe the Massachusetts requirements? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The pharmacist must determine what measures are appropriate in response to the DUR finding and may choose consultation with the prescriber, the patient, or the patient's agent when appropriate.
The pharmacist must document the measures taken in response to the DUR finding, not only a prescriber call.
A certified pharmacy technician may resolve the clinical conflict independently when an approved protocol supplies the decision steps.
Every DUR finding requires prescriber consultation before dispensing, regardless of the pharmacist's clinical assessment.
Documentation is optional when the pharmacist addresses the issue directly with the patient rather than the prescriber.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: Without patient authorization or another identified legal basis, a pharmacist sends a patient's complete medication profile through an encrypted portal to the patient's employer. The employer requested the profile for a workplace wellness review. Which statement best applies the Massachusetts licensee confidentiality duty?

choices.text: Encryption makes the transmission permissible because confidentiality duties address only accidental public exposure.
The pharmacist violates the affirmative confidentiality duty by sending the profile to an unauthorized recipient, despite using a secure channel.
The disclosure is permissible because an employer may request any medication information connected with a wellness program.
No confidentiality issue exists unless the employer later forwards the profile to someone else.
The duty is satisfied whenever the pharmacy protects its stored copy of the profile from unauthorized access.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is launching a monthly in-store injection service for a medication that Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer. The written protocol has the pharmacist complete the sale and hand the prefilled syringe to the patient at the register, has the patient carry it to the consultation room and hand it back unopened, and then has the pharmacist give the injection. The protocol assigns the patient no preparation, storage, or handling role, sets no interval between the handover and the return, and runs the same way for every patient. A staff pharmacist asks whether the protocol is acceptable. Which assessment is best?

choices.text: The formal characterization of the handover as a completed dispensing controls, so no administration restriction is engaged.
The patient's possession of the syringe makes the patient rather than the pharmacist the administering party.
The protocol is impermissible, because arranging the steps this way indirectly circumvents the administration restriction.
A valid prescription and a lawful dispensing together authorize the pharmacist to administer the medication.
Responsibility for the arrangement rests with whoever designed the protocol, not with the pharmacist following it.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives a medication after prescription processing was performed outside its premises at another pharmacy licensed by the Massachusetts Board. No separate Massachusetts pharmacist re-verifies that offsite processing at the receiving pharmacy. The pharmacist on duty inspects the finished medication before dispensing. Which assessment is most accurate?

choices.text: Dispensing is prohibited because every offsite process must be separately re-verified at the receiving pharmacy.
The Board-licensed offsite pharmacy satisfies an alternative condition for dispensing, without treating the final inspection as verification of the process.
The final inspection alone satisfies the rule, whether or not the offsite pharmacy is licensed by the Board.
The medication may be dispensed only if the offsite pharmacy also shares ownership with the receiving pharmacy.
The medication may be dispensed because any pharmacy license issued by any jurisdiction satisfies the offsite-site condition.

nearest_full_text_snapshots.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews a written Schedule II prescription before dispensing. The prescription contains the required patient, drug, strength, directions, and date information and bears the prescriber's signature, but it omits the practitioner's registration number. The filling pharmacist has already signed the face of the prescription. What is the best assessment?

choices.text: The prescription is complete because the pharmacist's face endorsement supplies the missing registration element.
The prescription is complete because a practitioner's signature makes a separate registration number unnecessary.
The pharmacist's endorsement satisfies the pharmacist's own duty but does not cure the missing practitioner registration number.
The missing registration number is cured if a second pharmacist countersigns the face before dispensing.
The registration number may be omitted from Schedule II prescriptions because they cannot be refilled.
